runtime_boundary: Represents the GenieX software runtime, not the Snapdragon silicon it targets and not Qualcomm AI Hub, the hosted model-compilation and device service from which pre-compiled bundles are fetched. The project was formerly published as NexaAI/nexa-sdk; that repository now redirects to qualcomm/GenieX, and the reviewed product name and owner are GenieX and Qualcomm, described in its own documentation as the community version of Qualcomm GENIE. It is not llama.cpp, which it vendors as a submodule and dispatches to, and not Qualcomm AI Engine Direct, the proprietary Qualcomm runtime reached through a separate plugin repository. Because the product exists to run models on the user's own device and its chat session and local server are how that capability is exercised, it classifies as a runtime rather than an assistant under ADR 015.
model_management: geniex pull downloads a model into a local cache from Hugging Face, Qualcomm AI Hub, Docker Hub, or a local directory or AI Hub zip archive, prompting for a GGUF precision where several exist and recording an inferred model type. geniex model list enumerates AI Hub models with a build for the detected chipset, geniex model set-type rewrites the cached manifest to switch between the language-only and multimodal load path, and geniex config get or set chipset controls chipset detection. Gated Hugging Face repositories are reached through GENIEX_HFTOKEN, HF_TOKEN, or the cached Hugging Face token file in that priority order. The local server does not auto-download; a model must be pulled first. No removal command is documented.
hardware_requirements: Execution is confined to Qualcomm Snapdragon; the documentation states there is no x86 or non-Snapdragon ARM build. The validated set is Snapdragon X Elite and X2 Elite on Windows ARM64, Snapdragon 8 Elite and 8 Elite Gen 5 on Android, and Dragonwing IQ-9075 and IQ-8275 on Linux ARM64, with chipset auto-detection on all three and an explicit chipset required for Qualcomm AI Hub pulls from the Android SDK. The llama.cpp runtime reaches the Hexagon NPU, the Adreno GPU through OpenCL, and the CPU, with a hybrid per-tensor Hexagon-plus-CPU scheduler and optional spreading across several HTP cores; the Qualcomm AI Engine Direct runtime is NPU-only and coerces other compute-unit requests with a warning. Python must be an ARM64 build.
operational_controls: A compute unit is selected per run as npu, gpu, cpu, hybrid, or an explicit HTP device list, and sampler and model flags including context length are set on the same command. Logging has six levels set by flag or the GENIEX_LOG environment variable. Speculative decoding is enabled with a draft model and draft-token bounds, and reports an accepted-draft ratio in the profiling block. The bundled server exposes a Swagger UI at its root and accepts any non-empty API key without checking it. Qualcomm AI Engine Direct bundles have precision, context length, and KV-cache size baked in and reject attempts to change them at runtime.
strengths: Two runtimes behind one interface give both breadth and depth on the same device: any community GGUF from Hugging Face runs on NPU, GPU, or CPU through llama.cpp, while Qualcomm AI Hub bundles run pre-compiled and pinned to the Hexagon NPU.
Model lifecycle is a complete product surface, covering pull from four sources, local cache, precision selection, chipset-aware listing, manifest editing, and gated-repository authentication.

The documentation is unusually specific about limits, naming the validated chipset list, the compute-unit alias mapping, the baked-in constraints of pre-compiled bundles, and the exact error returned when audio is sent to an unsupported runtime.
tradeoffs: Hardware coverage is deliberately confined to Qualcomm Snapdragon, so the runtime cannot serve any other fleet, and the Qualcomm AI Engine Direct path additionally requires a bundle compiled for the specific chipset.
Serving capability is interactive rather than concurrent: no batching, parallel-request handling, KV-cache management, or distributed serving is documented, and the server performs no authentication.
Observability is limited to log levels, a benchmarking tool, and per-run throughput output; there is no metrics or health endpoint for an operator.
The project is published as a developer preview, and the NPU path depends on proprietary Qualcomm runtime libraries rather than being open source end to end.
license_note: The repository publishes a BSD-3-Clause license file covering GenieX itself, and its NOTICE file lists bundled Go, C/C++, Python, and Android dependencies under MIT, Apache-2.0, and BSD terms, none of which restrict or alter the project's own license; bindings/python/LICENSE is a symlink to the same root file. The Qualcomm AI Engine Direct execution path, however, is not open source: the geniex-qairt submodule resolves to qualcomm/geniex-qairt-plugin, whose own third-party notices state that the QAIRT headers under qnn-api/ and the prebuilt Windows, Android, and Linux runtime libraries are proprietary Qualcomm Technologies code governed by the Qualcomm AI Runtime SDK end-user licence agreement and explicitly not relicensed under BSD-3-Clause. The README also states that use of the project is subject to Qualcomm's terms of use. An open-source product built around a proprietary accelerator runtime is a mixed_source boundary. The proprietary component is vendored as a git submodule, so its notices live in a separate repository and are recorded as dated web terms rather than a pinned blob in this record's own tree.
